Frédéric-Auguste Bartholdi. The French sculptor best known for conceiving and overseeing the creation of the Statue of Liberty, a gift from France to the United States. His monumental copper colossus stands 151 feet tall—a robed woman holding a torch—and has become the defining symbol of American liberty and immigration in New York Harbor since 1886.

Bartholdi designed the Statue of Liberty, officially called Liberty Enlightening the World, between 1875 and 1886. He collaborated with engineer Gustave Eiffel, who designed the iron framework that solved the technical challenges of creating a hollow copper statue at such unprecedented scale. The statue's face is said to have been modeled after Bartholdi's mother, and her broken chains symbolize freedom from tyranny.

Earlier in his career, Bartholdi sculpted public monuments and commemorative statues throughout France and Europe. He campaigned tirelessly to secure funding and support for the Liberty project, traveling to the United States and advocating for its completion. He created the conceptual vision of liberty as a maternal, welcoming figure—a powerful symbolic choice for a nation of immigrants. The torch and crown have guided countless people to American shores for over a century.
